usage: 불(을) 켜다 is the set phrase for lights; native speakers often drop 을 and just say 불 켜 줘.
Works for any screen device — TV, 컴퓨터, 모니터; the object takes 을/를.
to turn on the air conditioner
Same verb for appliances that 'run' on power; pairs with 끄다 to turn off.
켜다 also covers lighting a flame (촛불, 성냥불), since the original sense is 'bring a light to life'.
examples: 불 좀 켜 주세요.
Please turn on the light.
Simple request; 좀 softens it to 'a little / would you'.
방이 어두워서 텔레비전을 켰어요.
The room was dark so I turned on the TV.
Everyday cause-result; note the object particle 을 on 텔레비전.
회의 시작하기 전에 빔프로젝터를 켜 놓을게요.
I'll have the projector turned on before the meeting starts.
Real situation; 켜 놓다 = turn on and leave it on ready.
nuance: 켜다 means to bring a device, screen, or flame to life by supplying power, and it is the exact opposite of 끄다 (to turn off) — the two are always taught as a pair. The dividing line English speakers miss is 켜다 vs 열다: 열다 is physically 'to open' (a door, a box, a lid), so you must never say 텔레비전을 열다 for switching a TV on — that sounds like prying the set apart. 켜다 also is not 틀다, which Koreans use casually for playing media or running water (음악을 틀다, 물을 틀다); 켜다 focuses on the power state itself. It is a plain native verb (no 한자), neutral in register and fine in both 불 켜 줘 to a friend and 불을 켜 주시겠어요? to a stranger. The biggest pitfall: English 'turn ON' tempts learners toward 돌리다 (to spin/turn) — but there is no rotating image here, so 돌리다 is wrong. Habitual collocations are 불을 켜다, 텔레비전·컴퓨터를 켜다, 에어컨·히터를 켜다, and 촛불을 켜다.

mistakes: Saying 텔레비전을 열다 to mean 'turn on the TV' — 열다 is to open something physically, so this sounds like dismantling the set; use 텔레비전을 켜다.
Writing 켜어요 for the polite form — the 여 already contains the ㅓ sound, so it contracts to 켜요, never 켜어요.
Using 돌리다 because English says 'turn on' — 돌리다 means to rotate, which has no place here; the correct verb is 켜다.

usage: The set opposite of 불을 켜다; also literally 'to put out' a fire (불을 끄다 = extinguish flames).
Standard for powering devices down; 무음으로 하다 is different (just silencing, not off).
to turn off the air conditioner
Pairs with 켜다; 나갈 때 꼭 꺼 주세요 is a common sign in shared spaces.
Same verb for firefighters extinguishing a blaze — the root meaning is 'make the flame/light die'.
examples: 불 좀 꺼 주세요.
Please turn off the light.
Simple polite request with softening 좀.
잘 때 불을 끄고 자요.
I turn off the light before sleeping.
Everyday routine; -고 links two actions in sequence.
회의 중에는 휴대폰을 꺼 두시기 바랍니다.
Please keep your phone turned off during the meeting.
Formal real situation; 꺼 두다 = turn off and leave off.
nuance: 끄다 is the direct opposite of 켜다 and means to cut the power to a device or to extinguish a flame, so the same verb that turns off a lamp also 'puts out' a fire (불을 끄다 covers both). The conjugation is the key trap: 끄다 is a ㅡ-dropping (으 불규칙) verb, so when you add 아/어, the bare ㅡ vowel disappears and the ㅓ of the ending takes over — giving 꺼요 and past 껐어요, never 끄어요. English speakers also confuse 끄다 with 닫다 (to close): you 닫다 a door or app window, but you 끄다 the power; saying 컴퓨터를 닫다 wrongly means 'close the laptop lid', not 'shut it down'. Register is neutral — 불 꺼 to a friend, 불을 꺼 주시겠어요? to a superior. A subtler point: to merely silence a phone, Koreans say 무음으로 하다 or 진동으로 하다, not 끄다, because 끄다 means the screen goes fully dark. Natural collocations: 불·전등을 끄다, 핸드폰·컴퓨터를 끄다, 에어컨·히터를 끄다, 촛불을 끄다.

usage: The standard everyday phrase for brushing teeth — not 씻다; 양치(질)하다 is a synonym.
Wiping a flat surface clean with a cloth; pairs with 걸레, 행주, 휴지.
닦다 also means wiping moisture off — tears, sweat (땀을 닦다).
For leather shoes 닦다 means to shine/polish, often 구두를 닦다 at a shoe-shine stand.
examples: 이를 닦아요.
I brush my teeth.
Simple daily action; fixed collocation 이를 닦다.
밥을 먹고 식탁을 행주로 닦았어요.
After eating, I wiped the table with a dishcloth.
Everyday chore; 로 marks the tool 행주.
넘어진 아이가 눈물을 닦고 다시 웃었어요.
The fallen child wiped away the tears and smiled again.
Real scene; shows the 'wipe moisture' sense.
nuance: 닦다 is a hands-on cleaning verb that means to rub a surface to make it clean, dry, or shiny, and crucially it is the normal Korean word for brushing teeth — 이를 닦다 — even though English uses 'brush', not 'wipe'. The sharp contrast learners need is 닦다 vs 씻다: 씻다 means to wash with running water (손을 씻다, 얼굴을 씻다), so you 씻다 your hands but 닦다 your teeth, a table, or a window; mixing them up (이를 씻다) sounds odd to natives. 닦다 also differs from 청소하다, which is 'to clean a whole room/space' as a chore — you 청소하다 the house but 닦다 one specific surface. It is a plain native verb, neutral in register. Note the spelling: the stem ends in the double consonant ㄲ, so the present is 닦아요 (the ㄲ stays) and the formal is 닦습니다. Pitfall: do not import English 'clean' as one verb — Korean splits it into 닦다 (wipe/scrub a surface), 씻다 (wash with water), and 청소하다 (tidy a space). Common collocations: 이를 닦다, 창문·바닥을 닦다, 눈물·땀을 닦다, 구두를 닦다.

usage: For goods on offer; 여기서 표를 팔아요 = tickets are sold here.
Formal shop language; note ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다 → 팝니다.
싸게/비싸게 팔다 = sell at a low/high price; 게 turns 싸다 into an adverb.
중고로 팔다 = sell as a used item, very common for phones, books online.
examples: 여기서 표를 팔아요.
They sell tickets here.
Simple statement of what's on offer.
편의점에서 우산도 팔아요.
The convenience store sells umbrellas too.
Everyday availability; 에서 marks the place of selling, 도 'also'.
안 쓰는 옷을 중고로 싸게 팔았어요.
I sold clothes I don't use cheaply as secondhand.
Real situation; 중고로 + 싸게 collocation.
nuance: 팔다 means to sell — to hand over goods in exchange for money — and it is the natural opposite of 사다 (to buy), so the two are learned as a pair. The conjugation is the headline feature: 팔다 is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ 탈락) verb, meaning the stem-final ㄹ drops out before endings beginning with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ. That is why the formal present is 팝니다 (not 팔습니다) and the 'shall we' form is 팔까요? while ㄹ survives before vowels (팔아요, 팔았어요). The contrast to watch is 팔다 vs 판매하다: 판매하다 (販賣하다, 'sell-trade-do') is the Sino-Korean, formal/business equivalent you see on signs and in retail (온라인 판매), whereas 팔다 is the everyday spoken word. Register is neutral and native. A common English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the thing sold takes 을/를 (빵을 팔다), and you do not need a 'to'-phrase unless naming the buyer, who then takes 에게/한테. Do not confuse 팔다 with 팔리다, the passive 'to be sold / to sell well' (이 책이 잘 팔려요). Habitual collocations: 표·물건을 팔다, 싸게·비싸게 팔다, 중고로 팔다, 다 팔다(sell out).

mistakes: Writing 팔습니다 for the formal present — 팔다 is ㄹ-irregular, so ㄹ drops before -습니다 and the form becomes 팝니다.
Confusing 팔다 (to sell, active) with 팔리다 (to be sold / sell well) — say 책을 팔아요 to sell it, but 책이 잘 팔려요 for 'the book sells well'.
Marking the goods with the wrong particle — the item sold takes 을/를 (빵을 팔다); only the buyer takes 에게/한테.

usage: 도서관에서 책을 빌리다 — the source takes 에서 or 한테(서).
친구한테 돈을 빌리다; the lender (person) takes 한테/에게(서).
Opposite direction: 빌려주다 = lend; 펜 좀 빌려줘 = lend me a pen.
빌려 가다 / 빌려 오다 add direction — take a borrowed thing away or bring it back.
examples: 펜 좀 빌려주세요.
Please lend me a pen.
Simple request — note it's 빌려주다 (lend), what you say to the owner.
도서관에서 책을 세 권 빌렸어요.
I borrowed three books from the library.
Everyday action; 에서 marks the source institution.
보증금이 없어서 친구한테 돈을 좀 빌려야 했어요.
I had no deposit so I had to borrow some money from a friend.
Real situation; 한테 marks the person lender.
nuance: 빌리다 means to borrow — to take something with the understanding that you will return it (or, for money, repay it) — so it always implies a temporary, give-it-back relationship. The single biggest English-speaker trap is direction: 빌리다 is only 'borrow' (the thing comes TO you), while lending (giving it OUT to someone) is the separate verb 빌려주다, literally '빌리다 + 주다 (give)'. So '친구한테 책을 빌렸어요' = I borrowed a book from a friend, but '친구한테 책을 빌려줬어요' = I lent a book to a friend — the same 한테 changes meaning entirely depending on the verb. English 'borrow' and 'lend' are two words too, but learners reflexively use 빌리다 for both. The conjugation is regular (stem 빌리- + 어 → 빌려, past 빌렸어요). Watch the particles: the borrowed item takes 을/를, and the source takes 에서 for places (도서관에서) or 한테(서)/에게(서) for people. Register is neutral and native. Note also 빌리다 ≠ 임대하다/대여하다, the formal Sino-Korean for commercial renting (차를 대여하다). Common collocations: 책·돈·차를 빌리다, 도서관에서 빌리다, 빌려주다, 빌려 가다/오다.

Saying 빌려요 when you mean lending — to ask someone to lend you something, say 빌려주세요, not 빌리세요.

usage: Physically grasp a hand; 손을 꼭 잡다 = hold tightly.
Idiomatic 'grab' a cab on the street; 택시가 안 잡혀요 = can't catch one.
Safety phrase on buses/subways: 손잡이를 잡으세요.
Figurative — 약속·날짜·시간을 잡다 = pin down a plan/date.
examples: 손을 잡아요.
Hold my hand.
Simple physical action; fixed phrase 손을 잡다.
길에서 택시를 잡기가 어려워요.
It's hard to catch a taxi on the street.
Everyday difficulty; -기가 어렵다 = it is hard to.
다음 주로 회의 날짜를 잡았어요.
We set the meeting date for next week.
Real situation; figurative 날짜를 잡다 = fix a date.
nuance: 잡다 starts from the physical idea of closing your hand firmly around something — to grab, grasp, or hold — and from there fans out into many idioms Koreans use daily. The contrast to learn is 잡다 vs 들다: 들다 is to LIFT something up off a surface (가방을 들다 = pick up a bag), whereas 잡다 is to take HOLD of it without necessarily lifting (손잡이를 잡다 = grip the strap). It also differs from 쥐다, which is to clench in a fist (주먹을 쥐다); 잡다 is the broad everyday grip. Beyond the body, 잡다 means to CATCH (택시를 잡다 hail a cab, 도둑을 잡다 catch a thief, 물고기를 잡다 catch fish) and to SET/FIX a plan (약속을 잡다, 날짜를 잡다). The English pitfall is assuming 'grab' is purely physical and reaching for 가지다/들다 in the idioms — but 'catch a taxi' and 'set a date' both require 잡다 in Korean. It is a plain native verb, regular (잡아요, 잡았어요, formal 잡습니다), neutral register. Note the passive 잡히다 (be caught): 택시가 안 잡혀요. Common collocations: 손·손잡이를 잡다, 택시를 잡다, 약속·날짜를 잡다, 기회를 잡다.

usage: 문자·메시지·이메일을 보내다; the recipient takes 에게/한테.
For physical mail; 택배로 보내다 = send by courier.
Idiom — 즐거운 시간을 보내다 = have/spend a good time.
to send a child to school
Send a person somewhere; the destination takes 에.
examples: 친구에게 문자를 보내요.
I send a text to my friend.
Simple action; 에게 marks the recipient.
주소를 카카오톡으로 보내 주세요.
Please send me the address via KakaoTalk.
Everyday request; 으로 marks the means/channel.
방학을 시골 할머니 댁에서 보냈어요.
I spent the vacation at my grandmother's in the countryside.
Real situation; the 'spend time' sense of 보내다.
nuance: 보내다 means to send something or someone away from you toward another place or person — a message, a parcel, even a child to school — and it also carries the everyday idiom 시간을 보내다, 'to spend/pass time'. The sharp contrast is 보내다 vs 주다: 주다 (to give) is a face-to-face hand-over where giver and receiver are together, while 보내다 implies distance — the thing travels to reach the other person. So you 줘요 a gift you hand over now, but 보내요 a gift you mail; using 주다 for a text or parcel sounds like you are physically handing it across. The recipient particle is 에게/한테 (and honorific 께): 부모님께 보내다. For the 'spend time' sense, English speakers wrongly reach for 쓰다 (to use/spend money) — but time is 보내다, not 쓰다: 좋은 시간 보내세요! is the standard 'have a good time'. usage: Enter an enclosed space; the place entered takes 에 or 안에.
Idiom for heading home — 늦게 집에 들어가다 = get home late.
Figurative 'enter' a job/school — 대학에 들어가다 = get into university.
Of objects: 가방에 안 들어가요 = it won't fit in the bag.
examples: 안으로 들어가요.
Go inside.
Simple direction; 안으로 = toward the inside.
추우니까 빨리 안으로 들어갑시다.
It's cold, so let's go inside quickly.
Everyday suggestion; -읍시다 'let's'.
저는 보통 열한 시쯤 집에 들어가요.
I usually get home around eleven.
Real routine; the 'get home' idiom of 들어가다.

The crucial paired contrast is 들어가다 vs 들어오다: 들어오다 ('enter-and-come') is the same entering motion but TOWARD the speaker. So if you are inside a room and want someone to come in, you say 들어오세요 (come in), but if you are heading into a room over there, you 들어가요. English 'go in / come in' splits the same way, yet learners default to 들어가다 for both and tell a guest at their own door 들어가세요, which oddly means 'go away in / head on home'. Beyond the literal, 들어가다 idiomatically means to get home (집에 들어가다), to enter a school or job (대학·회사에 들어가다), and even 'to fit' (이 옷이 가방에 안 들어가요). usage: Leave an inside space; 밖에/밖으로 나가다.
Idiom — 매일 회사에 나가다 = go in to work each day.
to step out and come back
잠깐 나갔다 올게요 = I'll be back in a bit.
to attend/show up at a gathering
나가다 = turn up to a meeting/class (동호회에 나가다).
examples: 밖에 나가요.
I'm going outside.
Simple action; 밖에 = to the outside.
날씨가 좋아서 잠깐 나갔다 올게요.
The weather's nice, so I'll step out for a bit.
Everyday departure; 나갔다 오다 = go out and return.
다음 주부터 새 회사에 나가기로 했어요.
I've decided to start going in to the new company next week.
Real situation; 회사에 나가다 = report to work.

Idiomatically 나가다 also means to go (in) to work or attend a regular gathering — 회사에 나가다, 동호회에 나가다 — and even 'to be broadcast/aired' for media. Common collocations: 밖에 나가다, 회사·학교에 나가다, 나갔다 오다, 모임에 나가다.

usage: Move upward by stairs; the path takes 을/를 or 으로.
산에 올라가다; 정상까지 올라가다 = go up to the summit.
Figurative rise — 물가가 올라가다 = prices climb.
Koreans say 올라가다 for going to the capital from the provinces.

I go up.
Simple direction; 위로 = upward.
엘리베이터로 옥상까지 올라갈까요?
Shall we go up to the rooftop by elevator?
Everyday suggestion; 으로 marks the means, 까지 'all the way to'.
이번 달에 기름값이 많이 올라갔어요.
Gas prices went up a lot this month.
Real situation; the figurative 'rise' sense.
nuance: 올라가다 is 오르다/올라- (to rise, ascend) + 가다 (to go), literally 'rise-and-go' — to move UPWARD in a direction away from the speaker. Its mirror is 내려가다 (go down), and its toward-the-speaker partner is 올라오다 (come up). The contrast English speakers must internalize is 올라가다 vs 올라오다: if you are already upstairs and want someone below to join you, you say 올라오세요 (come up to me), but if you yourself are heading up, you 올라가요. Beyond the literal climb, 올라가다 is the everyday word for numbers RISING — 값·물가·온도·성적이 올라가다 (prices, temperature, grades go up) — so it competes with the more formal 상승하다 (上昇하다, used in news/finance). The path takes 을/를 or 으로 (계단을/계단으로 올라가다), the place 에 (산에). Pitfall: do not use 오르다 alone in casual speech for stairs — natives prefer the directional 올라가다. usage: Move downward by stairs; path takes 을/를 or 으로.
to go down to the first floor
Destination floor takes 으로 or 에.
From Seoul, going to a province is 내려가다 ('go down').
examples: 아래로 내려가요.
I go down.
Simple direction; 아래로 = downward.
짐을 들고 계단을 내려가야 해요.
I have to go down the stairs carrying luggage.
Everyday obligation; 을 marks the stairs as path.
약을 먹고 나니까 열이 조금 내려갔어요.

Real situation; the figurative 'drop' sense.

The contrast to lock in is 내려가다 vs 내려오다: standing downstairs and calling someone to join you, you say 내려오세요 (come down to me); heading down yourself, you 내려가요. usage: Return to a place toward the speaker; 에 marks the place.
to come back from a trip
Source of return takes 에서 (출장에서 돌아오다).
Opposite direction — return away from the speaker (고향에 돌아가다).
다시 reinforces the return; 곧 돌아올게요 = I'll be right back.
examples: 집에 돌아와요.
I come back home.
Simple action; 에 marks the destination of return.
출장에서 어제 돌아왔어요.
I came back from a business trip yesterday.
Everyday past; 에서 marks where you returned from.
일 끝나면 바로 집에 돌아올게요.
I'll come straight back home when work is done.
Real situation; -을게요 promise to the listener.
nuance: 돌아오다 is 돌다/돌아- (to turn, circle back) + 오다 (to come), literally 'turn-and-come' — to come BACK to a place, in a direction TOWARD the speaker or the home base. Its mirror is 돌아가다 ('turn-and-go'), returning AWAY from the speaker, and this is the central trap: if you are at home and tell family you'll be back, you say 집에 돌아올게요 (I'll come back here), but speaking of returning to your faraway hometown you say 고향에 돌아가다 (go back there, away). The destination of return takes 에 (집에 돌아오다), while the place you return FROM takes 에서 (여행에서 돌아오다). 돌아오다 also has the gentle idiom of things coming round again — 봄이 돌아오다 (spring returns), 기회가 돌아오다 (a chance comes back around).
